ch15_ex5_q1a: Quick quadrant test for angles between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ (not on an axis): divide by $90$, drop the decimal part and add 1. Here $60 \div 90 = 0.67$, giving quadrant 1.
$60^\circ$ is two-thirds of the way to vertical, so its point is high on the circle: $\sin(60^\circ) \approx 0.87$ is bigger than $\cos(60^\circ) = 0.5$.
ch15_ex5_q1b: Quick test: $130 \div 90 \approx 1.4$; drop the decimal part and add 1 to get quadrant 2.
$130^\circ$ is $50^\circ$ short of $180^\circ$, so its reference angle is $50^\circ$, measured from the negative $x$-axis.
ch15_ex5_q1c: Think of $310^\circ$ as $310^\circ - 360^\circ = -50^\circ$: turning $50^\circ$ clockwise from the positive $x$-axis lands you in quadrant 4.
ch15_ex5_q1d: $260^\circ$ is only $10^\circ$ short of $270^\circ$ (straight down), so its point is close to $(0, -1)$, just left of the negative $y$-axis.
ch15_ex5_q1e: Picture the radius as a clock hand: $100^\circ$ is $10^\circ$ past straight up, leaning left, so the point is just left of the $y$-axis in quadrant 2.
ch15_ex5_q1f: $185^\circ$ is only $5^\circ$ past $180^\circ$, so its point is very close to $(-1, 0)$: cosine is nearly $-1$ and sine is a small negative number.
ch15_ex5_q2: $43^\circ$ is just under $45^\circ$, so the triangle is almost isosceles: its legs $\cos(43^\circ) \approx 0.73$ and $\sin(43^\circ) \approx 0.68$ are nearly equal.
ch15_ex5_q3: Subtract from a full turn: $360^\circ - 295^\circ = 65^\circ$, so the radius is $65^\circ$ below the positive $x$-axis, in quadrant 4 with reference angle $65^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q4a: Small-angle estimate: $\sin\theta \approx \theta \times \frac{\pi}{180}$ for small angles, so $\sin(20^\circ) \approx 20 \times 0.0175 = 0.35$, close to the true $0.34$.
Benchmark check: $\sin(0^\circ) = 0$ and $\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5$, and $20^\circ$ is two-thirds of the way between them, so expect about $0.33$; the true value $0.34$ fits.
ch15_ex5_q4b: Check with Pythagoras on the unit circle: $\cos(20^\circ) = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2(20^\circ)} \approx \sqrt{1 - 0.34^2} \approx 0.94$.
$\cos(20^\circ) = \sin(70^\circ)$: the cosine of an angle is the sine of its complement.
ch15_ex5_q4c: $100^\circ$ is $10^\circ$ past vertical, so $\cos(100^\circ) = -\sin(10^\circ) \approx -0.17$, a small negative number because the point is just left of the $y$-axis.
ch15_ex5_q4d: $\sin(100^\circ) = \sin(80^\circ)$: angles the same distance either side of $90^\circ$ give points at the same height.
Pythagoras check with part c: $0.98^2 + 0.17^2 \approx 0.99$, which is about 1 as it should be.
ch15_ex5_q5a: Memory aid for positive ratios, quadrants 1 to 4: All Stations To Central (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).
ch15_ex5_q5b: $\cos(320^\circ) = \cos(40^\circ) \approx 0.77$, since a point and its reflection in the $x$-axis share the same $x$-coordinate.
ch15_ex5_q5c: Sanity check: the reference angle $35^\circ$ is a bit below $45^\circ$, so the size of the sine should be a bit below $\sin(45^\circ) \approx 0.71$; $0.57$ fits.
ch15_ex5_q5d: When the reference angle is below $45^\circ$ the point is closer to the $x$-axis, so $|\cos| > |\sin|$: here $0.82 > 0.57$.
ch15_ex5_q6a: Memory aid: the axis points are $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(-1,0)$, $(0,-1)$ at $0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ, 270^\circ$. Read cosine as the first number and sine as the second.
ch15_ex5_q6b: Since $\cos(90^\circ) = 0$, $\tan(90^\circ) = \frac{1}{0}$ is undefined. This is why the graph of $y = \tan(x)$ has a vertical asymptote at $90^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q6d: Half a turn sends every point to its opposite through the origin: $(1, 0)$ becomes $(-1, 0)$, so $\cos(180^\circ) = -1$.
On the graph of $y = \cos(x)$, $180^\circ$ is the lowest point of the wave.
ch15_ex5_q7a: On the graph of $y = \sin(x)$, $270^\circ$ is the minimum, three-quarters of the way through one cycle.
ch15_ex5_q7b: Pattern: cosine is 0 at every odd multiple of $90^\circ$ ($90^\circ, 270^\circ, 450^\circ, \ldots$), which is exactly where $\tan$ has its asymptotes.
ch15_ex5_q7c: Sine is 0 at every multiple of $180^\circ$ ($0^\circ, 180^\circ, 360^\circ, \ldots$) because those points lie on the $x$-axis.
ch15_ex5_q7d: Angles that differ by a multiple of $360^\circ$ give identical trig values, so $\cos(720^\circ)$ is also 1. Try it on your calculator.
ch15_ex5_q8a: Exact value: $\cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.866$, so a careful measurement should read about $0.87$.
Memory aid: the $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle has sides $1$, $\sqrt{3}$, $2$, so $\cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
ch15_ex5_q8b: Why it is exactly $\frac{1}{2}$: reflect P in the $x$-axis to P'. Triangle OPP' has two sides of 1 and a $60^\circ$ angle, so it is equilateral; PP' $= 1$, and $\sin(30^\circ)$ is half of it.
ch15_ex5_q9a: Quadrant 2 rule for the reference angle: $180^\circ - \theta$, so $180^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q9b: Exact value: $\cos(150^\circ) = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx -0.866$. The size comes from $30^\circ$ and the sign from quadrant 2.
ch15_ex5_q9c: General rule: $\cos(180^\circ - x) = -\cos(x)$ for every $x$, because the two points are mirror images in the $y$-axis.
ch15_ex5_q9d: The sine graph is symmetric about $x = 90^\circ$; $150^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ are both $60^\circ$ from $90^\circ$, so they have the same height.
ch15_ex5_q9e: General rule: $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin(x)$. Your calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ only ever returns the acute angle of such a pair, so you must find the other one yourself.
ch15_ex5_q10a: Quadrant 3 rule for the reference angle: $\theta - 180^\circ$, so $210^\circ - 180^\circ = 30^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q10c: General rule: $\cos(180^\circ + x) = -\cos(x)$. Adding half a turn sends the point through the origin to the opposite side.
ch15_ex5_q10d: Sine equals $\pm\frac{1}{2}$ at the four '30-type' angles: $+\frac12$ at $30^\circ, 150^\circ$ and $-\frac12$ at $210^\circ, 330^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q10e: General rule: $\sin(180^\circ + x) = -\sin(x)$. Together with part c, a $180^\circ$ rotation flips the sign of both coordinates.
ch15_ex5_q11a: Think of $330^\circ$ as $-30^\circ$: it is $30^\circ$ clockwise from the positive $x$-axis, so the reference angle is $30^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q11b: $\cos(330^\circ) = \cos(-30^\circ) = \cos(30^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$: cosine ignores the sign of the angle, because reflecting in the $x$-axis keeps $x$ the same.
ch15_ex5_q11c: General rule: $\cos(360^\circ - x) = \cos(x)$, which is why the cosine graph is symmetric about $x = 180^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q11d: Exact value: $\sin(330^\circ) = -\frac{1}{2}$, so no rounding is needed.
ch15_ex5_q11e: General rule: $\sin(360^\circ - x) = -\sin(x)$, the same as $\sin(-x) = -\sin(x)$.
ch15_ex5_q12a: Compare the three lengths for $20^\circ$: $\sin(20^\circ) \approx 0.342$, the arc length $20 \times \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.349$, and $\tan(20^\circ) \approx 0.364$. The vertical side is always the shortest of the three for an acute angle.
ch15_ex5_q12b: $\cos(20^\circ) = \sin(70^\circ)$: turn the $20^\circ$ triangle on its side and it becomes the $70^\circ$ triangle.
ch15_ex5_q12c: Why the tangent segment equals $\tan\theta$: the big triangle (base 1) is similar to the small one (base $\cos\theta$, height $\sin\theta$), so its height is $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.
ch15_ex5_q12d: Calculator technique: store $\sin(20^\circ)$ and $\cos(20^\circ)$ in memories (e.g. A and B) and compute $A \div B$, so nothing is rounded too early.
ch15_ex5_q12e: This is where the name comes from: $\tan\theta$ is a length along the tangent line to the circle at $(1, 0)$.
ch15_ex5_q13a: Exact value: $\sin(135^\circ) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.707$. The $45^\circ$ triangle has equal legs because both its acute angles are $45^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q13b: The point for $135^\circ$ is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$: coordinates of equal size but opposite sign.
ch15_ex5_q13c: Any angle whose radius lies on the line $y = -x$ ($135^\circ$ or $315^\circ$) has $\tan = -1$, because $\frac{y}{x} = -1$ on that line.
ch15_ex5_q13d: No calculation needed: equal sizes divide to give 1, and opposite signs make it $-1$.
ch15_ex5_q13e: Gradient view: $\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}$ is the gradient of the line OP. The line through O at $135^\circ$ slopes down to the right with gradient $-1$.
ch15_ex5_q13f: General rule: $\tan(180^\circ - x) = -\tan(x)$, because $\sin$ keeps its sign but $\cos$ changes sign.
ch15_ex5_q14a: The reference angle is $40^\circ$, so $\sin(220^\circ) = -\sin(40^\circ)$. That is why it has the same digits as $\sin(320^\circ) \approx -0.64$, which also has reference angle $40^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q14c: Sanity check: $40^\circ < 45^\circ$ and $\tan(45^\circ) = 1$, so $\tan(220^\circ) = \tan(40^\circ)$ must be a bit less than 1; $0.84$ fits.
ch15_ex5_q14d: Two negatives divide to give a positive, which is a quick way to remember why tan is positive in quadrant 3.
ch15_ex5_q14e: Gradient view: the radius at $220^\circ$ and the radius at $40^\circ$ lie on the same straight line through O, so they have the same gradient and the same tan.
ch15_ex5_q14f: General rule: $\tan(180^\circ + x) = \tan(x)$. This is exactly why tan has a period of $180^\circ$, not $360^\circ$.
ch15_ex5_q15b: Exact value: $\cos(300^\circ) = \cos(60^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}$, so no rounding is needed.
ch15_ex5_q15d: Exact working beats decimals: $\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = -\sqrt{3}$, with no rounding at all.
ch15_ex5_q15e: Gradient check: the radius at $300^\circ$ is steep and slopes down to the right, so its gradient should be a fairly large negative number, about $-1.73$.
ch15_ex5_q15f: General rule: $\tan(360^\circ - x) = -\tan(x)$, the tangent version of the quadrant 4 rule.
ch15_ex5_q16: Because the radius is 1, the triangle's legs are $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ themselves. On a circle of radius $r$ the point would be $(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$.
ch15_ex5_q17: Unit circle view: the point $(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$ lies on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, so this identity is Pythagoras in disguise.
ch15_ex5_q18: Another route: $\sin(180^\circ - \alpha) = \sin\alpha$ and $\cos(180^\circ - \alpha) = -\cos\alpha$; squaring removes the minus sign, so the statement becomes $1 - \sin^2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha$.
ch15_ex5_q19: The identity breaks down where $\cos\alpha = 0$ ($90^\circ, 270^\circ$), because both $\tan$ and $\sec$ are undefined there.
ch15_ex5_q20a: Draw a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and side $p$ opposite $x$; Pythagoras gives the adjacent side $\sqrt{1 - p^2}$.
ch15_ex5_q20b: Test with $x = 30^\circ$: $p = \frac12$ and $\sin(150^\circ) = \frac12$, which equals $p$ as expected.
ch15_ex5_q20d: In a right triangle the side opposite $x$ is the side adjacent to the other acute angle, $90^\circ - x$. So $\sin(x) = \cos(90^\circ - x)$.
ch15_ex5_q21: The points at $x$ and $180^\circ - x$ are mirror images in the $y$-axis, so they are at the same height and the difference is 0.
ch15_ex5_q22: The points at $x$ and $180^\circ - x$ have opposite $x$-coordinates, so the cosines cancel. Check: $\cos(60^\circ) + \cos(120^\circ) = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0$.
